cards.explanation: The answer is the loving devotion of the LORD. The writer says, “Because of the loving devotion of the LORD we are not consumed, for His mercies never fail.” After all that pain, he doesn't point to anything he built or earned. I think that's why hope can show up in the dark.

The answer is False. The word is “Your,” not “His,” so the writer is speaking straight to the LORD, not to his people. Verse 22 talks about Him, and verse 23 turns and talks to Him. That little shift is easy to miss, friends.

The answer is “My portion.” The soul says, “The LORD is my portion…” and then adds, “therefore I will hope in Him.” A portion is a share, the piece that's yours, friends. And the soul says that piece is the LORD.

The answer is those who wait for Him. The writer says, “The LORD is good to those who wait for Him, to the soul who seeks Him.” Waiting doesn't sound like much, friends, but he says it right out. He even calls it good to wait quietly in the very next verse.
The answer is LORD. The writer says, “Let him sit alone in silence, for the LORD has laid it upon him.” It's a heavy line, and I think it's worth sitting with. Notice who he names: the LORD.
The answer is True. After the face in the dust comes the line “…perhaps there is still hope.” I think this one hurts to read, friends. Then that little light shows up right behind it.

The answer is that the Lord will not cast us off forever. After the dust and the cheek, the writer says, “For the Lord will not cast us off forever.” The heavy part doesn't get the last word, friends. Verse 32 keeps going from there.

The answer is compassion. The verse says, “Even if He causes grief, He will show compassion according to His abundant loving devotion.” Grief is real in this poem, and the writer says so out loud. But compassion follows right in the same verse, tied to His abundant loving devotion. Hold onto that pairing, friends, because the verse puts the two side by side.

The answer is False. The verse says, “For He does not willingly afflict or grieve the sons of men.” The writer just said grief can happen, and now he adds that it isn't something He does willingly. That's a lot of comfort in one little word.

The answer is True. The writer lists crushing prisoners underfoot, denying a man justice, and twisting a man's lawsuit. Then he says, “…of these the Lord does not approve.” Those are heavy things, friends. He doesn't hedge, he just says it.

The answer is the Lord. The writer asks, “Who has spoken and it came to pass, unless the Lord has ordained it?” I once told a hot batch to cool faster, and that batch ignored me completely. The writer's answer is right in the question: the Lord. Nobody else in the verse gets that credit.

The answer is good. The writer asks, “Do not both adversity and good come from the mouth of the Most High?” He puts adversity and good side by side in one question. I think that's him saying both out loud, with no tiptoeing.

The answer is his sins. The writer asks, “Why should any mortal man complain, in view of his sins?” It's a sober question, friends, and I think it's meant to be read slowly. He asks it in the same poem that says the mercies are new every morning.
